title: Yellow Eyes
case: A 20-year-old man presents to your clinic with yellow eyes as shown.

qs.q: What further questions would you ask to elicit a diagnosis?
a: **Biodata:** name, age, sex, residence (malaria-endemic region); occupation (sex worker, health worker, farmer with exposure to pesticides, aflatoxins)
**HPI:** onset; does it last the whole day; associated abdominal pain, fever, weight loss, night sweats, constipation, vomiting, pale stools, dark urine, pruritus
Progression: has it become more yellow than before?
History of bilateral lower limb swelling?

**Risk factors:** IV drug use, recent blood transfusion, recent tattoos, family history of malignancy, excessive alcohol, excessive acetaminophen (paracetamol), smoking, travel to malaria-endemic regions, sickle cell disease
**Past medical history:** previous surgery and admissions, previous blood transfusion, history of drug use
**Family and social history:** anyone in the family with a similar condition

qs.q: State the possible investigations and expected findings depending on the aetiology.
a: **FBC:** low Hb (anaemia), low RBC count; WBC high if infection; low platelets (easy bruisability)

**LFTs:** total bilirubin high; direct and indirect may be high depending on whether the cause is pre-hepatic, hepatic or post-hepatic; GGT and ALP high in cholestasis; AST:ALT ratio (AST high in alcohol-induced, ALT high in hepatitis); albumin may be low
**Viral serology:** triple serology for hepatitis B/C and HIV; if hepatitis B: HBsAg, HBeAg, anti-HBs, HBV DNA copies
**Coagulation screen:** bleeding time prolonged; PT, aPTT, INR
**Imaging:** abdominal ultrasound (gallstones, mass, liver cirrhosis); CT abdomen-pelvis (staging and diagnosing malignancy); ERCP for gallstones and MRCP (obstructive jaundice)

title: The Hepatitis Serology Panel

Low detectable levels of HBV DNA because HDV RNA suppresses HBV DNA replication

title: The Stigmata of Chronic Liver Disease
case: A 65-year-old man presents to your clinic with the clinical signs shown.

qs.q: What is the possible diagnosis, with reasons?
a: Chronic liver disease, with the stigmata of chronic liver disease:
Easy bruisability, due to low clotting factors (vitamin K dependent: II, VII, IX, X)

qs.q: What are the possible causes of the condition shown above?
a: Infections: chronic hepatitis B and C, schistosomiasis, malaria

qs.q: State the long-term management of the condition above.
a: Specific medical therapies for many liver diseases, to diminish symptoms and forestall cirrhosis:
Interferon and other antivirals: hepatitis B and C
Ursodeoxycholic acid and obeticholic acid: primary biliary cholangitis
**Once cirrhosis develops, manage complications as they arise:**

Hepatorenal syndrome: kidney function usually recovers after liver transplantation; early cases may be salvaged by aggressive volume expansion with albumin and fresh frozen plasma and by avoiding diuretics
Ascites: sodium restriction, diuretics, large-volume paracentesis, shunts (peritoneovenous, portosystemic, TIPS)
**Liver transplantation:** refer for consideration after the first signs of hepatic decompensation

title: The Boy with a Distended Abdomen
case: A 12-year-old boy presents with anorexia, early satiety and a distended, non-tender abdomen. He has an enlarged liver and spleen, anaemia, leukopenia and thrombocytopenia on further examination.

qs.q: What are the possible causes of hepatomegaly in this patient? (VINDICATE)

qs.q: What are the causes of splenomegaly?

qs.q: State 5 possible causes.
a: **Vascular:** sickle cell anaemia, haemolytic anaemia, thalassaemias, CCF, cirrhosis, portal and splenic vein thrombosis

**Infectious:** malaria, kala-azar, infectious mononucleosis, tropical splenomegaly syndrome (hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly: immunological over-stimulation from repeated malaria over a long period)

qs.q: If the patient is from Eastern Province, what are the likely causes?
How would you go about evaluating this patient?
a: Take a complete history and do a full examination
FBC: evidence of infection, anaemia, thrombocytopenia (CML)
Peripheral blood film; thin and thick smears for malaria parasites
Blast cells for CML; bone marrow aspirate in case of CML
GeneXpert or Gram staining to rule out TB
Giemsa and Leishman staining: amastigotes on microscopy

title: Emergency Vivas: Gastroenterology
tag: Variceal bleed · Dysentery · Hepatic failure · Ascites
case: Short emergency management questions. Answer in a logical order: ABCs first.

qs.q: Management of an acute variceal bleed.
a: Assess haemodynamic status: BP and pulse
Put in an NG tube if the patient is aspirating
Take blood for GXM and grouping
Transfuse if Hb <7 g/dl (patients with comorbidities <8 g/dl)
Antibiotic prophylaxis: ceftriaxone 1 g 24-hourly for 7 days
Prepare for endoscopy within 12 hours of presentation: band ligation

qs.q: Give 4 possible causes of haematemesis.
Management of acute dysentery.
a: Fix 2 wide-bore IV cannulas; take blood for GXM and grouping
If in hypovolaemic shock: fluids (normal saline)
If Hb is low: prepare for transfusion with whole blood or packed cells
Stool samples to the lab for microscopy, culture and sensitivity
ORS for rehydration if needed, and zinc
Take a history and examine the patient once stable

qs.q: Management of acute hepatic failure.
a: Fix 2 wide-bore IV cannulas; take blood for GXM and grouping
Blood for FBC, coagulation profile, metabolic panel, LFTs
Protect the airway with an NG tube in case of aspiration
If encephalopathy and cerebral oedema: elevate the head, hyperventilate, mannitol, and give lactulose
If due to acetaminophen toxicity: N-acetylcysteine (antidote)
Ultrasound and CT once the patient is stabilised

qs.q: Management of ascites.
a: ABCs, fix 2 wide-bore IV cannulas, take blood for GXM
Blood for FBC, coagulation profile, LFTs, UECs, serum albumin
Ascitic tap (5 cm superior and medial to the ASIS, lateral to rectus abdominis, or 2 cm below the umbilicus): culture, microscopy, cell count, biochemistry
If albumin is low: albumin infusion
Manage complications: encephalopathy (lactulose); portal hypertension (propranolol; vasopressin and somatostatin)

title: A Cough, Breathlessness and Fever
case: A 62-year-old man presents to your clinic with a 2-week history of cough, shortness of breath, fever and fatigue. A chest radiograph taken at a local clinic demonstrated the findings shown.

qs.q: What further questions would you ask in the history to elicit your diagnosis?
a: **Cough:** onset, productive or not, colour of sputum, haemoptysis, worse at night, pleuritic chest pain, smelly sputum
**Shortness of breath:** onset, progressive, orthopnoea, PND, bilateral leg swelling, worse on exertion
**Fever:** onset, present throughout the day, night sweats, weight loss, loss of appetite
**Fatigue:** onset, chest pain, palpitations, headaches, syncope, bleeding disorders
**Risk factors:** overcrowded living, smoking, contact with people with similar symptoms, occupational exposure (cement, dust, pollen)
Alcohol intake (aspiration pneumonia); immunosuppression (malignancy, HIV, irradiation, benzene), corticosteroid use
Family history of cancer; trauma to the chest

qs.q: What other priority investigations would you order?
a: FBC: Hb, WBC count (neutrophil leukocytosis suggests bacterial, leukopenia viral)
Acute phase reactants: ESR, CRP, procalcitonin
Sputum staining and microscopy: ZN stain
GeneXpert on sputum to rule out TB
UECs, LFTs, BUN (>7 mmol/l suggests pneumonia)
CT chest and COVID-19 swab (ground-glass opacities)

qs.q: What would be your plan of management for this patient?
a: **Supportive:** oxygen for the desaturating patient, IV fluids, chest physiotherapy, pain relief (paracetamol), prop the patient up to 45 degrees
Antibiotics: ceftriaxone, or a macrolide, or a fluoroquinolone

title: Four Months of Cough, Night Sweats and Weight Loss
case: A 30-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of cough, night sweats, fever and weight loss. The chest radiograph is shown.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What investigations would you order?
a: Urine TB LAM antigen test (lipoarabinomannan assay: detects LAM, a component of mycobacterial cell walls, present mainly in active TB disease)

qs.q: What treatment regimen would you institute?
a: Give pyridoxine with isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy

qs.q: Give 3 differentials of the above presentation.

title: The Opaque Hemithorax
case: Look at the chest radiograph.

qs.q: What would be the expected clinical signs in this patient?
a: **General:** respiratory distress with accessory muscle use (nasal flaring, intercostal recession, SpO₂ <92%), central and peripheral cyanosis, asterixis
**Inspection:** chest moves asymmetrically (reduced on the affected side); tachypnoea; scars, distended veins, trauma; raised JVP in heart failure
**Palpation:** trachea shifts away from the effusion; apex beat diffuse; reduced chest expansion and reduced tactile fremitus on the affected side; palpate for chest wall masses
**Percussion:** stony dullness where the fluid is
**Auscultation:** reduced air entry and reduced breath sounds on the affected side; bronchial breath sounds; crackles or pleural friction rub may be heard; reduced vocal resonance

qs.q: Classify the causes of the above condition, and give 3 examples under each class.
a: **Transudative:** CHF, liver cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, hypoalbuminaemia, hypothyroidism
**Exudative:** pneumonia, malignancy, TB, pulmonary embolism, SLE, pancreatitis, viral or parasitic disease, rheumatoid arthritis

qs.q: What additional investigations would you order and why?
a: Imaging: CXR (PA and lateral) and CT chest
Pleural fluid analysis via thoracentesis: cell count, pH, LDH, protein, glucose, amylase, triglycerides, cholesterol, ADA, interferon, ANA
Culture and microscopy; ZN stain; urine LAM

qs.q: How would you manage the condition above?
a: **Supportive:** oxygen, prop up to 45 degrees, analgesia for chest pain
Manage the cause of the effusion
Chemical pleurodesis (doxycycline, bleomycin) in recurrent effusion

title: The Wasted Smoker
case: A 65-year-old known smoker presents with a 2-month history of dyspnoea and cough. Examination reveals pursed-lip breathing, and PA and lateral chest radiographs demonstrate the findings shown.

qs.q: What would be the other expected clinical signs in this patient?
a: **General:** respiratory distress (nasal flaring, accessory muscles, intercostal recession, cyanosis, SpO₂ <92%); finger clubbing, pallor, lymphadenopathy, nicotine tar stains, tremors, asterixis (CO₂ retention), oedema; muscle wasting
**Inspection:** hyperinflated, barrel-shaped chest; pursed-lip breathing; reduced chest movement bilaterally; raised JVP; wheeze; hoarse voice
**Palpation:** trachea central; apex beat may have shifted; reduced chest expansion; reduced tactile fremitus; palpable P2 (pulmonary hypertension)
**Auscultation:** diffusely decreased breath sounds; wheeze, crackles; reduced vocal resonance; distant heart sounds; loud P2

qs.q: What additional investigations would you order and why?
How would you manage the patient?
a: **Supportive:** oxygen if SpO₂ <92% with the patient propped up to 45 degrees; smoking cessation (counselling, nicotine replacement); prevent occupational exposure; vaccinations (influenza yearly, pneumococcal, COVID-19); chest physiotherapy
**Definitive:** if LRTI, treat with antibiotics (amoxicillin or doxycycline); oral prednisone in severe COPD
Group A: short-acting bronchodilator (SABA or SAMA) or a long-acting bronchodilator (LABD). SABA: fenoterol, salbutamol, terbutaline
Group B: LABA or LAMA (e.g. formoterol, salmeterol, tiotropium); if symptoms persist, LAMA + LABA
Group C: LAMA; for further exacerbation, LAMA + LABA or LABA + ICS (formoterol with budesonide)
Group D: LAMA + LABA; further exacerbation: LAMA + LABA + ICS; then consider macrolides (former smokers) and roflumilast if FEV1 <50% predicted with chronic bronchitis

title: Emergency Vivas: Respiratory
tag: Status asthmaticus · Inhalers · Oxygen therapy · Acute breathlessness
case: Short emergency management questions.

qs.q: Management of status asthmaticus.
a: Continuous nebulised albuterol/salbutamol with IV methylprednisolone
If no improvement: assess need for intubation; IV magnesium sulphate, epinephrine SC/IM, terbutaline
If improving: admit to ICU, continue primary therapy and reassess
**Severe:** salbutamol 4-8 puffs every 20 minutes in the first hour, with oral prednisolone 0.5-1 mg/kg
**Moderate and mild:** 2-4 puffs every 20 minutes in the first hour

qs.q: Prescribe medication to an asthmatic patient, giving instructions on inhaler and nebulizer use.
a: Budesonide-formoterol inhaler: combined reliever and controller
**Inhaler instructions (e.g. salbutamol):** shake the inhaler, breathe out, place the mouthpiece in the mouth, press and breathe in slowly, hold the breath, then wait before the next puff

qs.q: Briefly outline the principles of prescribing oxygen to patients in a hospital setting, and two adverse effects of high-flow oxygen.
a: Determine the need for oxygen therapy; obtain ABGs
Required flow rate for each condition
Target saturation 94-98% in acutely ill patients; for those at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure use a lower target
Administered by trained staff; make sure the right equipment is available (nasal prongs, non-rebreather mask)
Apply, then reassess: record oxygen saturation and the delivery system on the monitoring chart
Adjust devices and flow rates to keep saturation in the target range
Sign for oxygen on the drug chart each drug round
When discontinuing, reduce it in stable patients with satisfactory saturation; cross it off the drug chart once stopped
**Adverse effects of high-flow oxygen:** hyperoxaemia with oxygen toxicity; oxygen-induced hypercapnia (PaCO₂ >45 mmHg, V/Q mismatch)

qs.q: Give 6 differentials of acute shortness of breath.

title: The Deformed Hand
case: Look at the hand and its radiograph.

qs.q: State your diagnosis with reasons.
a: The X-ray shows large tophaceous deposits surrounding several joints of the right hand
Juxta-articular punched-out lytic erosions; erosions of joint margins with sclerosis

qs.q: State 4 risk factors of the condition above.
a: Diet high in uric acid (red meat, citrus)

qs.q: Priority investigations you would order to confirm your diagnosis.
a: FBC and acute phase reactants: ESR and CRP raised
Serum uric acid and urinary uric acid: raised
Synovial fluid analysis: birefringent monosodium urate crystals (gold standard)
X-ray, ultrasound, CT, MRI of the joint

qs.q: Definitive management of the condition shown.
a: NSAIDs (diclofenac, indomethacin, ibuprofen, celecoxib): first line
Colchicine 1.2 mg then 0.6 mg every 6-8 hours for several days, then taper
Corticosteroids (prednisone), after ruling out joint infection
More than 2 attacks/year, more than 1 tophus, joint erosion or urolithiasis: start urate-lowering drugs (allopurinol, or febuxostat if allopurinol-intolerant)
Lifestyle: reduce red meat, alcohol and seafood; increase low-fat dairy; lose weight; avoid dehydration

title: The Hands
case: Look at the hand and its radiograph.
figs: Radiograph of the hands and wrists

qs.q: State your diagnosis with reasons.
a: The image shows Bouchard's and Heberden's nodes
The radiograph of the hands and wrist joints shows reduced joint space, erosion of the articular margins, subchondral cysts and sclerosis
Diagnosis given in the key: rheumatoid arthritis

qs.q: What further history would you take from this patient?
a: **Risk factors:** family history; age (40s to 60s); sex (more common in women); smoking; genetic factors (HLA-DR4 and DR1); obesity; idiopathic

qs.q: State 5 priority investigations you would request and the expected findings.
a: FHG: raised ESR, CRP, procalcitonin; low Hb in severe cases (anaemia of chronic disease)
Synovial fluid analysis via joint aspiration: yellow, cloudy, leukocytosis, raised protein, reduced viscosity, rheumatoid factor
Imaging: plain radiograph of the joint, ultrasound, MRI

qs.q: Definitive management of the condition.
a: Acute attack: glucocorticoids, NSAIDs, selective COX-2 inhibitors
Long-term: DMARDs (hydroxychloroquine, methotrexate, sulfasalazine); drug of choice: methotrexate
Biological agents: adalimumab, infliximab, etanercept (TNF-alpha inhibitors)
Refer to a rheumatologist for complications

note: The source key names Bouchard's and Heberden's nodes (which point to osteoarthritis) but answers as rheumatoid arthritis. Confirm with your lecturer which diagnosis your examiners expect.

title: The Man Bent Over with Back Pain
case: A 30-year-old man presents with chronic back pain. He is bent over when presenting to accident and emergency. The radiograph ordered is shown.

qs.q: State your diagnosis with reasons.
a: X-ray: symmetrical fusion of articular surfaces; bamboo spine (syndesmophytes); loss of lordosis
The man is hunched forwards (kyphosis), cannot stand straight, with loss of the normal spinal curvature

qs.q: What further history would you take?
a: **SOCRATES** for the back pain: gradual onset of dull pain with morning stiffness that improves with activity; pain independent of position; also at night; tenderness over the sacroiliac joints; dactylitis can occur
Family history of the same condition (genetic: HLA-B27)
**Complications to ask about:** acute unilateral uveitis, restrictive lung disease from reduced mobility of the spine and thorax, chronic IBD, prostatitis

qs.q: What specific investigations would you order to confirm your diagnosis?
a: History, physical examination and pelvic X-ray (subchondral sclerosis and erosion)
FHG: low Hb (anaemia of chronic disease)

Chest expansion to assess severity; spine mobility testing (Schober's test: mark S1 and a point 10 cm above; on touching the toes without bending the knees, the distance should increase by at least 4 cm; less is pathological)
Mennell sign: tenderness on percussion and pain on displacement of the sacroiliac joints
FABER test: provokes pain in the ipsilateral hip

qs.q: Treatment.
a: **Medical:** first choice NSAIDs (indomethacin); additional TNF-alpha inhibitors (etanercept, infliximab, adalimumab); for peripheral arthritis use DMARDs (sulfasalazine)
**Surgery** to improve lifestyle: osteotomy, joint replacement, spinal fusion

title: The Echocardiogram
case: Look at the echocardiogram.

qs.q: State your diagnosis with reasons.
a: Mitral stenosis with a left atrial thrombus (the key notes: no stenosis, just a thrombus)

qs.q: What is the most common condition that causes this presentation?
What are other clinical signs and symptoms associated with that condition?
a: **Symptoms:** dyspnoea, palpitations, chest pain, fatigue, syncope
**Signs:** irregularly irregular pulse; heart murmurs; displaced apex beat; hyperactive precordium; ECG changes; apex-pulse deficit

**Acute rheumatic fever:** carditis (murmur, cardiac enlargement, CHF, pericardial effusion); migratory polyarthritis; Sydenham's chorea; erythema marginatum; subcutaneous nodules; history of sore throat and fever
**Rheumatic heart disease:** fatigue, dyspnoea, palpitations, haemoptysis, cough, oedema, ascites, chest pain; flushed cheeks (mitral facies), crepitations, diastolic murmur, loud P2

title: The Heroin Addict with Fever
case: A 27-year-old heroin addict is referred from a rehabilitation facility with the findings shown on echo imaging and clinical examination.
figs: Findings on the feet and hand

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What are the risk factors of the condition shown above?
a: Nosocomial or healthcare-associated IV devices (central lines, catheters)

qs.q: State the management of the condition above.
a: Investigations: blood cultures, echo (visible vegetations), 2D Doppler ultrasound, FBC, inflammatory markers; ECG
Emergency: stabilise the patient, oxygen, treat CCF, haemodialysis if needed
Antibiotics are the mainstay: IV penicillin G or IV ceftriaxone for 4 weeks; vancomycin if beta-lactam allergic
Surgical: valve replacement; prophylaxis before dental procedures and valve replacement (amoxicillin or ceftriaxone)

title: Fluid Overload and Cardiac Failure
case: The chest radiograph shown was taken in a 71-year-old woman with fluid overload and cardiac failure.

qs.q: State your diagnosis with reasons.
a: X-ray: diffuse airspace shadowing, generalised central consolidation, Kerley B lines
Diagnosis: pulmonary oedema secondary to left-sided heart failure

qs.q: State the acute management of the condition shown above.
a: Prop up the bed to 45 degrees
Inotropic agents if indicated (digoxin, dobutamine, norepinephrine)
Underwater seal chest drain if an effusion is present
**Monitor:** sodium and fluid restriction, input and output, physiotherapy

qs.q: Classify the condition shown above with examples.
a: Cardiogenic / hydrostatic / transudative: CHF, hypoalbuminaemia, cirrhosis

qs.q: Classify heart failure.
a: Heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (LVEF >50%)
Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (<40%)
Heart failure with mid-range ejection fraction (40-49%)

qs.q: Outline the management of heart failure in this patient.
a: ABCDs; oxygen if SpO₂ <92% (3.5-5 L/min); prop up to 45 degrees
ARB or ACE inhibitor: enalapril or losartan
Anticoagulation if at risk of thrombus (e.g. AF): enoxaparin
Ivabradine (lowers heart rate in sinus rhythm; selective SAN inhibitor)
**Monitor:** fluid restriction <1.5 L/day, salt restriction, daily weight at the same time of day

title: The Swollen Right Leg
case: A 35-year-old woman presents to your clinic with swelling of the right leg that is warm and tender to touch. She has a positive history of oral contraceptive use, but no history of smoking.

qs.q: What is the most likely diagnosis?
What questions would you ask in the history to enable you to clinch the diagnosis?
a: **Biodata:** name, age, occupation (inactive desk job, pilot)
**Presenting complaint:** swelling of the right leg
**HPI:** onset, site, progression; pain with movement; warmth; skin changes such as redness; difficulty walking
Associated features: syncope, pleuritic chest pain, unexplained dyspnoea

**Risk factors:** recent surgery (hip fracture, knee replacement), trauma, chemotherapy or active cancer within 6 months, long-distance travel, bedridden >3 days post-op, smoking, oral contraceptive use, recent pregnancy, CHF, previous VTE

qs.q: What priority investigations would you order to confirm your diagnosis?

title: Emergency Vivas: Cardiology
tag: Myocardial infarction · Warfarin bleed · Severe hypertension
case: Short emergency management questions.

qs.q: Outline the initial management of a patient with acute myocardial infarction.
a: Prop up the patient to 45 degrees
Connect to an ECG monitor; monitor every 15 minutes
Fix 2 large IV cannulas; take blood for FBC, LFTs, RFTs, RBS, lipid profile, thyroid function
Morphine 5 mg for pain; sublingual nitrate
Cardiac biomarkers (troponin T and I) on admission and after 4 hours

qs.q: A patient who was on warfarin after heart valve surgery 2 months ago presents with massive bleeding through the nose, mouth and rectum. How would you manage this patient?
a: Hold the warfarin until the cause of the bleeding is found, regardless of INR
Fix 2 IV cannulas; take samples for FBC, GXM, coagulation profile (INR), LFTs, UECs (in case of AKI)
Give crystalloid or colloid to replace volume loss while awaiting blood

**Bleeding:** stop warfarin regardless of INR; vitamin K 10 mg IV once; prothrombin complex concentrate (factors II, VII, IX, X): pre-treatment INR 2-4 give 25 IU/kg, INR 4-6 give 35 IU/kg, INR >6 give 50 IU/kg; if unavailable give FFP 10-15 ml/kg IV once; monitor INR every 4 hours until ≤1.1

**Not bleeding (asymptomatic):** INR above therapeutic but <5: decrease dose or stop warfarin, monitor INR every 24 hours, restart at the same or a lower dose once in range; INR >5 but <10: stop warfarin, monitor INR every 24 hours, give oral vitamin K if bleeding risk is increased, restart 10-15% lower once INR normal; INR >10: stop warfarin, give high-dose oral vitamin K, monitor INR every 24 hours, repeat oral vitamin K if still elevated at 24 hours

Urinary cortisol and dexamethasone suppression test

qs.q: Classify the condition above.
a: **Massive:** acute PE with sustained hypotension (haemodynamic instability)
**Submassive:** systolic BP >90 mmHg with either RV dysfunction or myocardial necrosis

qs.q: Management of the condition above.
a: **Supportive:** ABCDEs; bed rest in the acute stage; oxygen if hypoxic; 2 large-bore IV cannulas; IV saline to maintain venous pressure in massive embolus; analgesia

**Mainstay:** enoxaparin SC, or unfractionated heparin IV; start warfarin from day 1 with daily INR monitoring (effect takes 5 days); rivaroxaban if the patient can afford it
